reasoning_content: The goal is to show that the coercion of a nested infimum of intervals equals the nested intersection of the coerced intervals. The left side is `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)`. The right side is `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The lemma `Interval.coe_iInf` states that for any function `g : ι → Interval α`, the coercion of its infimum equals the intersection of the coerced intervals: `↑(⨅ i, g i) = ⋂ i, ↑(g i)`. Applying this lemma to the outer infimum (with `g := fun i => ⨅ j, f i j`) rewrites the left side to `⋂ i, ↑(⨅ j, f i j)`. Then applying the same lemma again to the inner infimum (with `g := f i` for each `i`) rewrites each `↑(⨅ j, f i j)` to `⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. This yields the right side exactly. Therefore, `simp only [coe_iInf]` suffices, as it will apply the lemma twice, once for each infimum.

The goal is to show that the coercion of a double infimum of intervals equals the double intersection of their coerced sets. The inner expression `⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j` is a double infimum over two indices. The lemma `Interval.coe_iInf` states that the coercion of an infimum of intervals equals the intersection of their coerced sets. Applying this lemma once would rewrite `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)` to `⋂ i, (⨅ j, f i j : Set α)`. The inner term `⨅ j, f i j` is itself an infimum, so applying the lemma again inside the intersection rewrites each `(⨅ j, f i j : Set α)` to `⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. This yields the right-hand side `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The `simp` tactic can apply the lemma twice in a single step because it simplifies the entire expression recursively, using the lemma's `simp` attribute.

The goal is to show that the coercion of a double infimum of intervals equals the double intersection of the coercions of those intervals. The left-hand side is `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)`. The right-hand side is `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The lemma `Interval.coe_iInf` states that for a single index, the coercion of an infimum equals the intersection of the coercions. Applying this lemma once would rewrite `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)` to `⋂ i, ↑(⨅ j, f i j)`. Then applying the same lemma again inside the intersection would rewrite each `↑(⨅ j, f i j)` to `⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`, resulting in `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`, which matches the right-hand side. Therefore, `simp [iInf, Interval.coe_iInf]` suffices: `iInf` expands the double infimum into a single infimum over a product type, and `Interval.coe_iInf` handles the coercion of that single infimum.

The goal is an equality between the coercion of a nested infimum of intervals and a nested intersection of the coerced intervals. The left-hand side is `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)`. The right-hand side is `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The inner infimum `⨅ j, f i j` is an infimum over `j : κ i` of intervals. The lemma `Interval.coe_iInf` states that the coercion of an infimum of intervals equals the intersection of the coerced intervals. Applying this lemma to the inner infimum transforms the left-hand side to `↑(⨅ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j))`. Now the outer infimum is over `i : ι` of sets (since each `⋂ j, ↑(f i j)` is a set). The same lemma `Interval.coe_iInf` applies again, converting this to `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`, which matches the right-hand side exactly. The `simp` tactic with `coe_iInf` will apply this lemma twice, once for each infimum, simplifying the goal to a trivial equality.
